table.title: Customer Onboarding Field Validation Rules
table.html:
FieldPatternExample validError message
account_email^[A-Za-z0-9.!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+@[A-Za-z0-9](?:[A-Za-z0-9-]{0,61}[A-Za-z0-9])?(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9](?:[A-Za-z0-9-]{0,61}[A-Za-z0-9])?)+$mira.okafor@northwind-logistics.co.ukEnter a complete email address, including the domain (for example, name@company.com).
phone_e164^\+[1-9]\d{7,14}$+442079460958Use international format: a plus sign followed by 8–15 digits, with no spaces, hyphens, or parentheses.
postal_code_us^\d{5}(?:-\d{4})?$94107-2231Enter a 5-digit ZIP code or ZIP+4 (for example, 94107 or 94107-2231).
effective_date^\d{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])-(0[1-9]|[12]\d|3[01])$2024-02-29Use YYYY-MM-DD; the month must be 01–12 and the day 01–31.
currency_amount^(?:0|[1-9]\d{0,8})(?:\.\d{2})?$12500.00Enter a non-negative amount up to 999,999,999.99 with two decimal places; omit commas.
slug^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$quarterly-compliance-reviewUse lowercase letters, numbers, and single hyphens only; do not start or end with a hyphen.
eu_vat_id^[A-Z]{2}[0-9A-Z]{8,12}$DE811234567Enter the country code followed by 8–12 letters or digits, without spaces.

d1.purpose: Provide a reference for validating customer onboarding fields, with a pattern, valid example, and user-facing error message for each field.
tasks: Find a field and read its validation rule, example, and error message across the row.
Compare patterns and constraints across fields when implementing or checking validation.
Read error messages and examples to understand the expected input.
relations: Each row connects one field identifier to its regex, a valid value, and the message shown when validation fails.
The example and error message explain the same constraints expressed more compactly by the regex.
roles: The first column identifies rows; the remaining columns contain the pattern, example, and error message for each field.
The header labels each column; the seven body rows have equal structural importance.
keep_whole: Field identifiers, regex tokens and syntax, example values, numbers, and meaningful units such as YYYY-MM-DD where space permits.
The long email regex is wider than a phone viewport even before the other columns are included.
may_wrap: Error messages can wrap at natural word boundaries.
Patterns and long examples may need to wrap at available break points in compact layouts, with some identifiers or tokens splitting in a viewport-fitting layout.
same_scale: All field identifiers share one column scale; examples and error messages should each remain consistent within their own columns.
Pattern and prose columns need different widths because their content and reading tasks differ.
d1.h_vs_v: Fitting all four columns on a phone makes every column narrower than its longest unbreakable content and produces extensive splitting and tall rows. Scrolling preserves identifiers and gives examples and messages usable reading widths, at the cost of moving horizontally to connect information across each row.

d2.purpose: Document validation rules for customer onboarding fields, pairing each field's pattern with a valid example and a corrective error message.
tasks: Find a field and inspect its validation rule.
Compare a pattern with its valid example.
Read the error message to understand how to correct an invalid value.
relations: Each row links one field to its regular expression, example and error message.
Examples illustrate the patterns; error messages explain the requirements in reader-facing language.
roles: Field names are row headers and lookup keys.
Example valid supplies concrete test values.
keep_whole: Field identifiers, example values and meaningful regex tokens should stay intact wherever space permits.
Digits, punctuation and character order in patterns and examples must remain legible.
may_wrap: Error messages can wrap at natural word boundaries.
Long regular expressions may wrap, though breaks make them harder to inspect.
In a viewport-fitting table, long identifiers and examples may need to split.
same_scale: Field names and examples benefit from compact but sufficient widths for their identifiers.
Pattern and error message columns need more space, with their relative widths determined by whether code inspection or prose reading is the priority.
d2.h_vs_v: A fitting table avoids horizontal scrolling but forces severe breaks and tall rows. Scrolling buys legible identifiers, examples and prose; additional pattern width can greatly reduce the height of the long email rule, at the cost of more horizontal travel.

d3.purpose: Document validation rules for customer onboarding fields, connecting each field’s pattern to a valid example and an error message.
tasks: Find a field and inspect its validation rule.
Compare the rule with a valid example.
Find the error message presented when a value fails validation.
relations: Each row connects one field to its pattern, example and error message.
The example illustrates the pattern; the error message explains the expected input to a user.
roles: Field is the row label and lookup key.
Example valid is a concrete input value.
Error message is explanatory prose; the column headers identify these distinct roles.
keep_whole: Field identifiers, example values, dates, phone numbers, email addresses and other machine-readable tokens should stay whole where space allows.
Regular-expression syntax should remain continuous and preserve every character; arbitrary breaks make it harder to inspect and copy.
may_wrap: Error messages can wrap between words and at natural phrase boundaries.
Long patterns may need to wrap when width is constrained, although the email expression is especially costly to accommodate on one line.
same_scale: All field labels share one visual role, as do all examples and all error messages.
Pattern and error-message columns can be wider than the field column because they contain more complex material.
d3.h_vs_v: A viewport-width table avoids horizontal scrolling but forces identifiers, examples and patterns to break, producing tall rows. A wider table preserves meaningful units and supports comparison, at the cost of scrolling across each row; accommodating the entire email pattern on one line requires especially extensive scrolling.

analysis.strengths: Field names, examples and headers remain whole. The initial viewport shows the complete field and pattern columns, supporting field-to-rule lookup. The table is considerably shorter and more readable than the fitting layouts.
analysis.faults: The long email pattern wraps across six lines, making its structure harder to trace and creating an unusually tall first data row. Examples and error messages require horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: It gives the field column its full required width, keeps the pattern column just inside the initial viewport, and reserves generous space for examples and prose.

analysis.strengths: All four columns are visible without horizontal scrolling. Its relatively wide field column makes some identifiers easier to recognize than in S.
analysis.faults: Identifiers, examples, prose and a header break inside words. The narrow pattern column produces a 23-line cell and an exceptionally tall table, making comparisons across rows difficult.
analysis.spatial_logic: It divides the viewport fairly evenly, with a modest preference for field names and error messages. That leaves too little usable text width in every column.

analysis.strengths: Field names, examples and headers remain whole, while the wider pattern column makes most expressions easier to inspect. The long email rule occupies only three lines, producing the most compact and even row rhythm shown.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through the pattern column, so several rules cannot be read without scrolling; examples and messages are farther away still. Its extra width offers diminishing returns for shorter patterns.
analysis.spatial_logic: It preserves P's generous field, example and message widths and spends another 180 px on patterns, trading horizontal travel for shorter, more legible rules.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible at once. Its wider pattern column reduces the longest cell to 17 lines and makes it the shortest of the fitting layouts.
analysis.faults: Field identifiers are heavily fragmented, undermining row lookup; examples and messages also split inside words and numbers. Despite the shorter first row, the table remains very tall and difficult to scan.
analysis.spatial_logic: It shifts space from the field column to the pattern column, accepting broken row labels to reduce regex wrapping.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible, and its comparatively wide field column keeps some shorter identifiers intact. The pattern column limits the longest cell to 17 lines.
analysis.faults: The example and message columns are especially narrow, breaking headers, words, numbers and examples into fragments. Its three-line header and tall rows weaken hierarchy and scanning.
analysis.spatial_logic: It favors field names and patterns over examples and messages, but the remaining widths are too small for continuous reading.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve the table's essential lookup units far better. P makes the field and full pattern column available together on first sight, while R improves regex inspection and row rhythm at the cost of more horizontal travel. The fitting layouts expose every column but fragment the very identifiers, values and messages the reader needs to compare; S's lower height comes with a particularly costly loss of row-label legibility. None of the proposed widths has been rendered, so their actual wrapping and relative quality remain to be checked.

analysis.strengths: Field names remain whole, headers fit on one line, and the initial viewport contains the field and pattern columns. The narrower table reduces horizontal travel.
analysis.faults: The email pattern occupies six lines, while its valid example wraps across two. Examples and error messages require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The 210 px pattern column fits beside the field column in the initial viewport, prioritizing field-to-pattern lookup over compact rows.

analysis.strengths: The wider pattern column keeps several expressions on one line, and the email example remains whole. The first row is shorter than in s0A.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through longer patterns, and the wider table increases travel to examples and messages. The email pattern still spans five lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: Extra width improves the full-table reading but makes the first view less self-contained than s0A.

analysis.strengths: All four columns are available without horizontal scrolling, and the field column is wider than in S.
analysis.faults: Field identifiers, examples, headers, and error-message words are broken across lines. The email pattern reaches 17 lines, producing a very tall table and making row comparison difficult.
analysis.spatial_logic: Four narrow columns preserve simultaneous visibility at the cost of continuous reading and dense vertical scanning.

analysis.strengths: The first viewport contains the complete field and pattern columns, and the wider example column keeps the email address on one line. Headers and field identifiers remain whole.
analysis.faults: The email pattern still takes six lines, and examples and messages are initially offscreen. The extra example width adds horizontal travel compared with s0A.
analysis.spatial_logic: It combines a self-contained initial field-and-pattern view with an unwrapped example column farther right.

analysis.strengths: The email pattern takes three lines, several shorter patterns fit on one line, and examples remain whole. Rows are more even and the full table is easier to scan vertically.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through several patterns; reaching examples and messages requires the most horizontal travel of the candidates.
analysis.spatial_logic: A wide pattern column improves code reading in the full table, trading away a complete first-screen view of that column.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible at once, and the headers wrap more cleanly than in s0C. It is shorter and has fewer measured word breaks than s0C.
analysis.faults: Field identifiers, examples, numbers, and message words still break awkwardly. The email pattern reaches 17 lines, and tall rows leave large empty regions in neighboring cells.
analysis.spatial_logic: A little width moves from field and pattern toward examples and messages, improving the fit relative to s0C but fragmenting the lookup labels further.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve identifiers and provide substantially better reading conditions. P is strongest when a complete field-and-pattern view on arrival matters; R is stronger for reading patterns after scrolling. S is the better fitting candidate by the measured breaks and height, though both fitting layouts severely fragment important content. The 359 px width budget cannot accommodate the minimum unbroken widths of all four columns, so further fitting refinements must choose which content to protect.

analysis.strengths: The wider field and error columns give some labels and messages more room than the other fitting layouts. The whole table is visible without horizontal scrolling.
analysis.faults: Field identifiers, example values, error messages and regexes break inside meaningful units. The Example valid header itself breaks within a word. The email row is exceptionally tall, and reading across any row requires tracking through large areas of empty space.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow example column sacrifices values to give the field and message columns more room, but it is too narrow to support either reliable examples or a compact row rhythm.

analysis.strengths: The example column is more generous than in s1B, and both multiword headers wrap without splitting their words.
analysis.faults: Identifiers, examples and messages still split awkwardly, and the narrow pattern column produces the tallest email row of the group. At 2221px, the table is the longest fitting candidate.
analysis.spatial_logic: A more even distribution gives the examples space at the expense of patterns and messages. That exchange increases row heights without protecting the long values.

analysis.strengths: Field names and headers are whole, examples fit on one line, and messages read naturally. The first viewport shows the complete field and pattern columns, which makes field-to-rule lookup especially useful. The table is substantially shorter than the fitting candidates.
analysis.faults: The long email regex wraps to six lines, making its syntax harder to follow. Examples and messages require horizontal scrolling, and the field label is no longer visible when the reader reaches the far right.
analysis.spatial_logic: The field and pattern widths together almost exactly fill the first viewport. This creates a useful initial view while keeping the remaining columns broad enough for readable content.

analysis.strengths: The wider pattern column makes most regexes easier to scan and reduces the email rule to three lines. Whole identifiers, examples and natural message wraps produce a compact, orderly full table.
analysis.faults: The first viewport cuts through several regexes, so their apparent shortness in the full view does not translate into complete first-sight reading. The larger scroll distance also separates fields from examples and messages.
analysis.spatial_logic: Extra width is concentrated in patterns, improving the full-table view at the cost of the useful column boundary that P places at the viewport edge.

analysis.strengths: It is the shortest fitting candidate and gives the email regex more room than s1B or s1C. Both multiword headers wrap without breaking their words.
analysis.faults: Field identifiers are severely fragmented, including currency_amount over three lines. Examples and messages also split within words and values; the shorter overall height does not make those fragments easy to read.
analysis.spatial_logic: Space shifts from fields to patterns, reducing the dominating email row but weakening the row labels needed to locate every rule.

rounds.insights: The 360px constraint is too tight to preserve the table's identifiers, examples, code and prose simultaneously. Among fitting layouts, S reduces height, while s1B better protects field labels; neither is comfortable for lookup. Scrolling permits much stronger readability, but the initial viewport matters: P presents complete fields and patterns together, whereas R makes patterns shorter in the full table while cutting them off at first sight. The email regex is the main reason to consider extra pattern width, so its benefit should be weighed against that loss of context.

analysis.strengths: Fits the viewport and keeps each row's four cells visible together. The field column is wider than in S, helping some identifiers.
analysis.faults: Identifiers, examples, error messages and regex fragments break at awkward points. The split Example valid header and very tall rows make scanning difficult.
analysis.spatial_logic: A modest preference for the field column leaves the example and message columns too narrow; the resulting vertical expansion overwhelms the benefit of seeing all columns at once.

analysis.strengths: Field names remain intact, headers fit on one line, and the wider pattern column makes several regexes easier to inspect. Prose wraps into manageable lines.
analysis.faults: The email example wraps, and the first viewport cuts through the pattern column, hiding both the examples and messages. The long email regex still spans five lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: Space favors patterns, but the initial viewport shows neither the whole pattern column nor a glimpse of the next column. The wide pattern column also leaves substantial unused space in shorter rows.

analysis.strengths: The first viewport contains the complete field and pattern columns. Examples, including the email address, stay on one line, and wider messages produce a more compact table.
analysis.faults: The email regex spans six lines, and several shorter patterns wrap where they remain whole in s2C. Examples and messages require horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first two columns nearly fill the viewport, creating a useful initial lookup view. More width goes to examples and messages, trading some pattern readability for shorter rows.

analysis.strengths: Fits the viewport, is slightly shorter than s2A, and gives examples and messages a little more room.
analysis.faults: The narrow field column fragments identifiers such as currency_amount and postal_code_us. Examples, prose and regexes also break awkwardly, and rows remain extremely tall.
analysis.spatial_logic: Redistributing a small amount of width reduces height but damages the row labels that anchor lookup. All four columns remain too narrow for their content.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve identifiers and readable text far better. P has the strongest initial viewport because the field and pattern columns fit together; s2C makes patterns easier to inspect but cuts them at the viewport edge. Among fitting layouts, s2A better protects row labels, while S is shorter at a substantial cost to lookup. Neither fitting layout avoids severe fragmentation, so further width changes should test which content deserves priority rather than expect a fully readable four-column fit.

bad.why: The fitting layout splits field names, examples and ordinary words across lines; the narrow example column also breaks its header.
The example column fragments identifiers and breaks its header across three lines, while error messages are difficult to read in the narrow final column.
The narrow pattern column turns the email expression into 23 lines, and the other columns still split identifiers, examples and prose.
Both multiword headers break inside words, and the narrow example and error columns fragment values and prose.

contrast.why: Equal widths appear orderly but disregard the columns' different content: field identifiers, regexes, examples and messages all fragment, making lookup and comparison laborious.

synthesis.rationale: Layout P keeps field names and examples whole, gives error messages a comfortable measure, and shows the complete field and pattern columns at the initial viewport position. Layout S is the strongest fitting candidate by the supplied measures, but its split identifiers, values and prose are serious compromises; it is a finalist only within the required fitting class. The other scrolling candidates remain publishable, although s3A wraps the email example, s2C narrows the prose, and R demands considerably more horizontal travel.

general: Allocate width according to content and lookup tasks rather than equalizing columns with different roles.
Preserve identifiers, values and meaningful units where possible, and judge the initial viewport as well as the full scrollable table.
Treat fewer lines as a benefit only when the added width does not unduly hinder navigation.
specific: A 147 px field column keeps these row labels whole.
P's 210 px pattern column fits alongside the field column in the initial viewport, though the long email expression still wraps across six lines.
No fitting candidate keeps this table's identifiers, examples and messages consistently intact.

synthesis.tradeoffs: P requires 583 px of horizontal scrolling to reach the far edge. R reduces pattern wrapping but increases that distance to 763 px. S avoids horizontal scrolling but is nearly 2,000 px tall and breaks important text; it should be accepted only if fitting the viewport is a hard requirement.
synthesis.uncertain: The preferred scrolling width depends on whether readers more often inspect complete regexes or move between patterns, examples and error messages. The supplied views do not establish how easily users discover horizontal scrolling or retain row context while scrolling.

critique.good: All four columns are visible at once, preserving the row relationships without horizontal scrolling.
critique.problems: Field names, examples, regexes, and messages break into fragments. The exceptionally tall first row and uneven row heights make scanning and comparison difficult; two headers also wrap.
critique.cause: All four columns are too narrow for their content. The 90 px pattern column produces a 22-line email regex, while the 85 px field and 88 px example columns split identifiers and values; the 96 px message column fragments prose.

critique.good: Field identifiers and headers remain whole, and the more compact total width reduces horizontal travel compared with C. Messages generally read in coherent phrases.
critique.problems: The email regex occupies nine lines and dominates the first row; several other patterns and examples wrap. At first sight only the field, pattern, and a sliver of the example are visible, so reading across requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 180 px pattern column is narrow for regex comparison, and the 188 px example column wraps the email and slug. The 776 px table extends well beyond the viewport.

critique.good: Examples stay whole, most patterns are readily scanned, and messages wrap naturally. Shorter, more regular rows make comparison easier.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the pattern column and shows neither examples nor messages. The large horizontal span makes connecting a field to its message laborious; wide columns also leave considerable empty space in shorter rows.
critique.cause: The 420 px pattern, 285 px example, and 360 px message columns produce a 1213 px table. The pattern width improves regex reading but puts the remaining columns far from the field identifiers.

critique.good: Complete field identifiers, mostly compact patterns, and comfortably readable messages make this the strongest reference layout. The wider example column keeps the slug on one line, and the row heights support comparison.
critique.problems: The email example still wraps, and the first viewport cuts through the pattern column; examples and messages require substantial horizontal scrolling. The long email pattern remains difficult to follow across five lines.
critique.cause: The 260px pattern column exceeds the space remaining beside the 147px field column in the initial viewport. The 220px example column is narrower than the full email example.

critique.good: All four columns are visible together without horizontal scrolling, and the field column gives identifiers slightly more room than d1r0A.
critique.problems: Identifiers, examples, regex syntax, and prose fragment across lines. The email row is extremely tall, making it hard to follow and compare rows; the narrow columns also leave large vertical gaps beside shorter cells.
critique.cause: Widths of 100, 85, 78, and 96px leave too little text space for the contents, particularly in the pattern and example columns.

critique.good: Field identifiers remain whole, headers fit on one line, and the narrower table reduces horizontal travel compared with d1r1A. Messages remain reasonably readable.
critique.problems: The email regex occupies nine lines and dominates the first row; other patterns also wrap more often. The slug example wraps, while the initial viewport shows only a sliver of the example column.
critique.cause: The 180px pattern column makes the long regex very tall, and the 188px example column is too narrow for the complete slug. The first two columns together nearly fill the viewport.

critique.good: All columns are visible at once, and the slightly wider pattern and example columns reduce some fragmentation compared with d1r1B.
critique.problems: Several field identifiers split, as do regex tokens, examples, and words in messages. The very tall email row and uneven empty space make lookup and cross-row comparison laborious.
critique.cause: The 85px field column cannot hold the longest identifiers, while the 90px pattern, 88px example, and 96px message columns are all too narrow for continuous reading.

critique.good: Field identifiers are whole, headers are clear, and the initial viewport shows the complete field and pattern columns. Messages wrap at readable boundaries.
critique.problems: The email pattern occupies six lines, and several shorter patterns wrap. The email example breaks across lines. Examples and messages require horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 210 px pattern column constrains regexes, while the 220 px example column cannot keep the longest email on one line.

critique.good: The wider pattern column keeps more short expressions on one line, and the 285 px example column keeps the long email example whole. Messages are comfortable to read.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through several patterns, and the table requires substantial horizontal travel to reach the error messages. The date range 01–12 breaks across lines.
critique.cause: The 300 px pattern column extends well beyond the space left beside the field column; the 320 px message column happens to wrap at the date range.

critique.good: All columns are visible without scrolling, and the wider field column improves some identifiers over d1r0A.
critique.problems: Headers, identifiers, examples, and ordinary words split repeatedly. The narrow message column produces extremely tall rows and makes cross-row comparison difficult.
critique.cause: At 105, 100, 74, and 80 px, every column is narrower than important unbreakable content, especially the example and message columns.

critique.good: It reduces the email pattern to five lines while preserving whole field identifiers and readable messages. Its total width is more restrained than d1r2B.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through patterns; the email example wraps, and the email regex remains difficult to follow across lines.
critique.cause: The 260 px pattern column exceeds the initial space remaining after the field column, and the 220 px example column is too narrow for the full email.

critique.good: All four columns are visible, and its more even allocation gives examples and messages somewhat more room than d1r2C.
critique.problems: Identifiers, patterns, example values, and message words split throughout. The first row is particularly tall, making the table laborious to scan.
critique.cause: The 85 px field and 90 px pattern columns are too narrow for their contents; 88 and 96 px also leave examples and prose severely constrained.

critique.good: Field identifiers, examples and headers remain whole. The first viewport shows the complete field and pattern columns, making initial lookup straightforward.
critique.problems: The email pattern occupies six lines, and several shorter patterns wrap. The wide example column leaves substantial empty space in most rows.
critique.cause: The 210 px pattern column is narrow for regex reading; the 285 px example column is sized for the longest email.

critique.good: The wider pattern column reduces the email regex to four lines and keeps several shorter patterns on one line. Error messages read comfortably.
critique.problems: The email example wraps, and the first viewport cuts through most patterns. The table requires the most horizontal travel of the candidates.
critique.cause: The 330 px pattern column extends beyond the initial viewport; the 220 px example column cannot keep the email example on one line.

critique.good: All four columns are visible together without horizontal scrolling, preserving the row relationships at a glance.
critique.problems: Identifiers, examples, prose and regex syntax split repeatedly. The email row is exceptionally tall, and the narrow columns make both lookup and comparison laborious.
critique.cause: The 100, 75, 78 and 106 px columns each fall well below the space needed for their longest unbreakable content.

critique.good: The complete field and pattern columns appear in the first viewport. Identifiers remain whole, and this is the narrowest scrolling candidate.
critique.problems: The email pattern takes six lines, several other patterns wrap, and the email example breaks across lines. The long first row creates considerable empty space beside the pattern.
